title: Absence of lateral domain wall mobility in Zn1-xMgxO thin films
authors: Jack Eckstein, Kyle P. Kelley, William Prudnick, Jon-Paul Maria, Stephen Jesse, Neus Domingo, Rama K. Vasudevan
abstract: Polarization reversal in ferroelectrics arises from the coupled processes of domain nucleation and subsequent growth, yet the governing mechanisms differ fundamentally between classical perovskite oxides and emerging wurtzite ferroelectrics. While switching in perovskites is typically governed by mobile domain walls whose field-driven propagation dominates macroscopic kinetics, here we show that polarization reversal in wurtzite Zn1-xMgxO proceeds through a qualitatively different pathway. Using scanning oscillator microscopy, in combination with point pulse-imaging methods, we directly map local switching events and domain wall responses, revealing that domain walls in Zn1-xMgxO exhibit negligible lateral mobility (sub 10nm) and that polarization reversal proceeds predominantly through the nucleation of vertically extended columnar filaments with a lateral size on the order of the grains. This nucleation-controlled switching contrasts sharply with the growth-mediated dynamics characteristic of perovskite ferroelectrics and explains the abrupt, spatially localized switching behavior observed in wurtzite systems. These results establish nucleation-dominated filamentary reversal as a defining switching mechanism in Zn1-xMgxO and point towards the need for further studies to understand correlation lengths and nucleation processes across a range of grain sizes.
summary: This work investigates the mechanism of ferroelectric switching in $	ext{Zn}_{1-x}	ext{Mg}_x	ext{O}$ thin films, finding that the process is governed by nucleation rather than the lateral movement of domain walls. Using advanced microscopy and modeling, the authors demonstrate that domain walls exhibit negligible mobility, establishing a new, nucleation-dominated switching mechanism for wurtzite ferroelectrics.
main_problem: The study compares the mechanisms of polarization reversal (switching) in wurtzite ferroelectrics ($	ext{Zn}_{1-x}	ext{Mg}_x	ext{O}$) versus classical perovskite ferroelectrics.
main_result: Polarization reversal in $	ext{Zn}_{1-x}	ext{Mg}_x	ext{O}$ is found to be dominated by the nucleation of vertically extended columnar filaments, as lateral domain wall mobility is negligible ($<10	ext{nm}$).
method: The research employs advanced local characterization techniques, including scanning oscillator microscopy and point pulse-imaging, complemented by detailed simulations.
model_or_system: The system is $	ext{Zn}_{1-x}	ext{Mg}_x	ext{O}$ thin films, which are wurtzite ferroelectrics. The analysis contrasts their switching behavior with that of perovskites, modeling the switching process as nucleation-controlled rather than growth-mediated.
key_observables: Local switching events, domain wall responses, lateral domain wall displacement, and the comparison of switching kinetics between wurtzite and perovskite systems.
important_parameters: Lateral domain wall mobility (shown to be sub 10 nm), coercive field, and grain size (mean size $\sim 10	ext{ nm}$).
main_assumptions: The simulations often neglect elastic and depolarization effects, and the analysis of wall position relies on subtracting electrostatic contributions from the raw measurement signal.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate that when lateral wall motion is disabled in simulations, the results match experimental observations of multiple unswitched grains, supporting the nucleation-dominated model.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the fundamental difference in switching mechanisms between perovskites (growth-dominated) and wurtzites. It then uses SO-PFM and pulse-probe methods to experimentally prove the lack of lateral wall movement in $	ext{Zn}_{1-x}	ext{Mg}_x	ext{O}$, culminating in simulations that confirm nucleation-limited switching.
why_interesting: While the core physics is ferroelectrics, the rigorous, quantitative measurement of domain wall dynamics using advanced microscopy techniques (SO-PFM) and the comparison to theoretical models of phase transitions make it relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in condensed matter.
